pos: proper noun (a region of Asia Minor)
etymology: Greek Pamphylia, perhaps “of all tribes,” a coastal region of southern Asia Minor; the district through which Paul passed on his missionary journeys.
biblical_def: Pamphylia was a coastal region of southern Asia Minor, lying between Lycia and Cilicia, with Perga as its chief inland city and Attalia as its port. It figures in the Acts as a district Paul traversed in his missionary labours. On the first journey, when Paul and his company loosed from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia, and there John Mark departed from them and returned to Jerusalem—a withdrawal that later occasioned the sharp contention between Paul and Barnabas. Returning from the highlands of Pisidia, they preached the word in Perga and went down to Attalia. Devout men from Pamphylia were among the multitude at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost who heard the wonderful works of God in their own tongue. And in his last voyage Paul sailed over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia on his way as a prisoner to Rome. The dictionary notes Pamphylia chiefly to ground the apostolic mission in real and traceable geography, and for one solemn lesson it carries: it was at Perga in Pamphylia that John Mark forsook the work, and this defection became the occasion of a painful breach between two faithful men. Yet the grace of God restored Mark, who is later commended as profitable for the ministry and became the writer of a Gospel. Pamphylia thus witnesses both to the cost of turning back from the Lord's work and to the mercy that restores the fallen servant who is recovered to usefulness.
webster_summary: A coastal region of southern Asia Minor, with Perga its chief city, traversed by Paul on his journeys (Acts 13:13; 14:24); the place where John Mark forsook the work, occasioning a breach later healed by grace.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the critical doubt cast on the historical reliability of Acts' geography and the loss of the moral lesson of Mark's defection and restoration.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the historical reliability of the book of Acts. Skeptical scholarship has often treated Luke's travel narratives as loose or legendary, but the precise and verifiable geography—Pamphylia, Perga, Attalia, the sea-lanes to Myra—has repeatedly been vindicated, and Luke stands as a careful and accurate historian. The dictionary affirms the trustworthiness of the sacred record: the apostolic mission unfolded in real places that can be traced on a map.

Pamphylia also carries a moral lesson the dictionary will not pass over. It was at Perga that John Mark forsook the work and returned to Jerusalem, a defection so serious that Paul refused to take him on the next journey, and the disagreement parted Paul and Barnabas. Yet the story does not end in failure: Mark was restored, and Paul at the last called him profitable for the ministry. The dictionary marks both edges—the real cost of turning back from the Lord's service, and the grace that recovers the fallen servant and makes him useful again. The young man who left the work in Pamphylia became, by mercy, the writer of a Gospel.

etymology: Greek Machairous, from machaira (a sword or dagger); the hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea, the traditional and historical site of John the Baptist's imprisonment and beheading.
biblical_def: Machaerus was the fortress-palace of Herod Antipas, perched on a height east of the Dead Sea in Perea, the place where, according to the historian Josephus and the constant tradition of the church, John the Baptist was imprisoned and beheaded. The Gospels do not name the fortress but record the events that took place there. Herod had laid hold on John and bound him in prison for Herodias' sake, his brother Philip's wife, whom he had unlawfully married, because John had told him plainly, “It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife.” Herodias nursed a quarrel and would have killed him, but feared the people and Herod's own reverence for the just and holy man. The occasion came at Herod's birthday feast, when the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him, and he swore to give her whatsoever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she demanded the head of John the Baptist in a charger; and the king, sorry yet bound by his oath and his guests, sent an executioner, who beheaded John in the prison. The dictionary marks Machaerus as the scene of a martyrdom that displays the courage of the faithful prophet who would not flatter a king's sin, the murderous power of a guilty conscience and a vengeful woman, and the folly of the rash oath that snared a weak ruler into innocent blood. John, of whom the Lord said none greater had been born of women, died in a dungeon for the truth, the forerunner sealing in blood the testimony he bore in life.
webster_summary: Herod Antipas' hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea, the historical site of John the Baptist's imprisonment and beheading (Mark 6:17-27); the scene of a martyrdom that exposes guilty power, a vengeful queen, and a rash oath.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the modern flattery of power that excuses what John condemned, and the loss of the prophet's example of fearless reproof.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prophet's duty to reprove sin even in the seats of power. John the Baptist lost his head because he told a king plainly, “It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife.” The modern instinct, eager to flatter the powerful and to call all private arrangements nobody's business, would have counselled John to silence. The dictionary holds up his example: the faithful witness names sin as sin, whatever the cost, and does not trim the word of God to please a Herod.

Machaerus also exposes the anatomy of a weak and guilty soul. Herod feared John, heard him gladly, and did many things; yet he kept his unlawful wife, bound himself with a drunken oath, feared the opinion of his guests more than the blood of a righteous man, and so was trapped into murder. The dictionary marks the lesson: the man who will not part with his cherished sin will be driven by it to worse, and the fear of man and the rash vow are snares that have destroyed many. John's martyrdom, sealed in that grim fortress, stands as the crown of a life that feared God and not the king.
roots_summary: From the Greek machaira (a sword or dagger); the fortress is named by Josephus as the place of John's death, confirmed by the church's tradition.

pos: proper noun (a city; the second Rome)
etymology: Greek Konstantinoupolis, “the city of Constantine,” founded A.D. 330 on the site of Byzantium; the imperial capital of the Eastern Roman Empire and a chief seat of the early church.
biblical_def: Constantinople was the city founded by the emperor Constantine in A.D. 330 on the site of ancient Byzantium, the “New Rome” that became the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire and one of the great centres of the early and medieval church. Though not named in Scripture, it figures large in the history of Christ's church. There the Second Ecumenical Council met in A.D. 381, completing the Nicene Creed—the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed—which confessed the full deity of the Holy Spirit, who proceedeth from the Father, against the Pneumatomachian heretics, and reaffirmed the deity of the Son against lingering Arianism. Nearby Chalcedon in 451 defined the two natures of Christ. The dictionary honours Constantinople as the place where the church, contending earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints, set down in enduring words the orthodox doctrines of the Trinity and the person of Christ—that the Word was God, and that God was manifest in the flesh. Yet the dictionary does not idealize the city. It became the seat of the Eastern Orthodox patriarchate, and from it spread errors the Reformation would later call the church away from: the veneration of icons (defended at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787), an increasingly sacramental and sacerdotal religion, and the eventual schism with the West in 1054. The dictionary thus honours Constantinople for its great service in defining Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy, while marking the departures of Eastern Orthodoxy from the Scriptural faith—preserving what was preserved there, and naming as error what later grew there contrary to the Word of God.
webster_summary: The city of Constantine (founded A.D. 330), capital of the Eastern Roman Empire and seat of the Council of 381 that completed the Nicene Creed; honoured for defining Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy, while its later Orthodoxy's errors are named.

corruption_summary: Constantinople preserved Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy, yet became the seat of Eastern Orthodoxy's icon-veneration, sacerdotalism, and the eventual schism—departures from the Scriptural faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary honours Constantinople for genuine and lasting service to the truth: the Council of 381 there completed the Creed that confesses the deity of the Son and the Spirit, and the church of the East long preserved the great Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy against the Arian and Pneumatomachian heresies. What was preserved there—the Word who was God, God manifest in the flesh, the Spirit proceeding from the Father—the dictionary affirms without reservation. Here the church earnestly contended for the faith once delivered to the saints, and the whole church remains in its debt.

Yet the dictionary will not idealize the city or the Eastern Orthodoxy that grew from it. From Constantinople and the councils it influenced came the veneration of icons, sanctioned at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which the dictionary names a corruption of the second commandment; an increasingly sacerdotal and sacramental religion that obscured justification by faith alone; and the great schism of 1054 that divided East from West. The dictionary's posture toward Eastern Orthodoxy is that which the voice-lock prescribes: respect what is preserved—Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy and the patristic heritage—and name what departs—icon-veneration, eucharistic theology, and an ecclesial structure that does not bow to Scripture alone.

etymology: From Antioch in Syria; the early Christian school of biblical interpretation marked by literal, historical, and grammatical exegesis, in contrast to the allegorical method of Alexandria.
biblical_def: The Antiochene school was the early Christian tradition of biblical interpretation centred at Antioch in Syria—the city where the disciples were first called Christians—distinguished by its attention to the literal, historical, and grammatical sense of Scripture, in contrast to the allegorical method that prevailed at Alexandria. Where the Alexandrians, following Origen, sought hidden spiritual meanings beneath the plain words and often dissolved the history into symbol, the Antiochenes insisted on the historia, the real events and the author's intended sense, reading prophecy and type in their grounding in genuine history. The dictionary commends the Antiochene instinct as broadly sound and akin to the historical-grammatical method the Reformers recovered: Scripture has one true sense, to be drawn out by attention to its words, grammar, and historical setting, and read as the apostles read it, with Christ as its scope. The greatest fruit of the school was John Chrysostom, the “golden-mouthed” preacher whose expository sermons through whole books of the Bible remain a model of careful, text-driven preaching. Yet the dictionary does not idealize the school. Its method, pressed without the safeguards of the rule of faith, contributed in some hands to error: Theodore of Mopsuestia and especially Nestorius, products of the Antiochene tradition, so divided the natures of Christ as to fall into the Nestorian heresy condemned at Ephesus. The dictionary therefore commends the literal-historical method as the right foundation, while insisting it be governed by the analogy of faith and the catholic creeds, lest a true principle of interpretation be turned, by neglect of the whole counsel of God, into a doorway for heresy.
webster_summary: The early Christian school of interpretation at Antioch, marked by literal, historical, and grammatical exegesis against Alexandrian allegory; sound in method (its fruit Chrysostom), yet in some hands (Nestorius) leading to Christological error.

corruption_summary: The Alexandrian allegory the Antiochenes opposed dissolved the historical sense into symbol; yet the Antiochene method, unguarded by the rule of faith, bred the Nestorian division of Christ's natures.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief error the Antiochene school rightly resisted was the runaway allegory of Alexandria, which, following Origen, sought hidden spiritual meanings beneath the plain text and often treated the history as mere husk to be discarded for the kernel of symbol. The dictionary sides with the Antiochene instinct, and with the Reformers who recovered it: Scripture has one true sense, grounded in real history and the author's intent, to be drawn out by grammar and context and read with Christ as its scope. Allegory unmoored from the literal sense becomes a tool by which any meaning may be imposed on any text.

Yet the dictionary marks the opposite danger that grew within the Antiochene tradition itself. A method that rightly honours the distinct historical realities can, pressed without the governing rule of faith and the catholic creeds, over-divide; and so Theodore of Mopsuestia and especially Nestorius so separated the two natures of Christ as to teach two persons, the heresy condemned at Ephesus in 431. The dictionary's conclusion is balanced: the literal, historical, grammatical method is the sound foundation of all faithful interpretation, but it must be governed by the analogy of faith and the orthodox confession of Christ, lest a true principle become, by neglect of the whole counsel of God, a doorway to error.

etymology: The second chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, recording the outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost and the birth of the New Testament church.
biblical_def: Acts 2 is the chapter recording the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost and the public birth of the New Testament church. When the day of Pentecost was fully come, the disciples were all with one accord in one place, and there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and cloven tongues like as of fire sat upon each of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost and spake the wonderful works of God in the tongues of the gathered nations. Peter, standing with the eleven, preached the first Christian sermon, declaring that this was the fulfilment of Joel's prophecy—“I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh”—and proclaiming Jesus, crucified and risen, as both Lord and Christ. Pricked in their hearts, the hearers cried out, and Peter answered, “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.” That day about three thousand souls were added, and they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, in breaking of bread, and in prayers. The dictionary holds Acts 2 as a foundational and unrepeatable event in redemptive history: the promised Spirit was poured out, the gospel went forth in power, and the church was constituted. It marks the chapter against two errors. The Pentecostal movement treats Pentecost as a pattern to be normatively repeated, expecting tongues and a “second blessing” for all; the dictionary holds Pentecost to be a once-for-all turning-point, like the cross and resurrection, whose abiding fruit is the indwelling Spirit given to all believers. The opposite error neglects the chapter's plain marks of a true church—apostolic doctrine, fellowship, the ordinances, and prayer—which remain the pattern for the church in every age.
webster_summary: The chapter recording the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost, Peter's sermon, and the birth of the church, with three thousand added (Acts 2:1-42); a foundational, unrepeatable event whose fruit is the indwelling Spirit and the marks of a true church.

“Repent, and be baptized… and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost” (Acts 2:38).

corruption_summary: Pentecostalism treats Pentecost as a normatively repeatable pattern of tongues and second-blessing, while others neglect the chapter's abiding marks of a true church.
corruption_paragraphs: The Pentecostal and charismatic movements read Acts 2 as a normative pattern to be repeated in every believer's life—a “baptism in the Spirit” subsequent to conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues. The dictionary, holding the cessationist Reformed position, regards Pentecost rather as a foundational, once-for-all turning-point in redemptive history, like the incarnation, the cross, and the resurrection, which inaugurated the age of the Spirit. Its abiding fruit is the Spirit given to indwell all believers (Acts 2:38-39), not a repeatable second experience reserved for some. The tongues of Pentecost were known languages, a sign for that pivotal hour, not the universal mark of a higher Christian class.

The opposite neglect overlooks what Acts 2 establishes as the abiding pattern of a true church. The three thousand who were added did not merely have an experience; they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine, in fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers. The dictionary holds these four marks—apostolic teaching, true fellowship, the ordinances, and prayer—as the perpetual shape of the church Christ built. Acts 2 is thus both the record of an unrepeatable founding event and the charter of the ordinary, abiding life of the church in every age.

etymology: The first epistle of the apostle John, a pastoral letter written that believers might know they have eternal life and walk in light, love, and truth.
biblical_def: First John is the first of the three epistles of the apostle John, a pastoral letter written to assure true believers and to guard them against the early errors that denied the incarnation. John opens with the witness of an eyewitness to the Word of life—“which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes… and our hands have handled”—grounding the faith in the real, bodily coming of the Son of God against the Gnostic and proto-docetic teachers who denied that Christ had come in the flesh. The epistle weaves together great themes: God is light, and the believer walks in the light, confessing sin and cleansed by the blood of Christ, our advocate with the Father; God is love, and he that loveth not knoweth not God; and the believer is called to love the brethren in deed and truth. John gives a series of tests by which a soul may discern whether its profession is true—obedience to the commandments, love of the brethren, and confession that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh—and states his purpose plainly: “These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life.” The dictionary holds First John to be the great epistle of Christian assurance, teaching that the believer may have real and settled knowledge of his salvation, grounded in the finished work of Christ and confirmed by the marks of true faith. It marks the book against two errors: the perfectionism that twists “he that is born of God sinneth not” into sinlessness in this life, when John also says that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves; and the cheap assurance that claims to know God while walking in darkness and hating the brethren, which John flatly denies.
webster_summary: The apostle John's first epistle, grounding the faith in the eyewitnessed incarnation against early error, and teaching the tests of true faith; the great epistle of Christian assurance (1 John 5:13)—“that ye may know that ye have eternal life.”
webster_full: 1 JOHN, proper noun. The first epistle of the apostle John, a pastoral letter of assurance and truth.
It grounds the faith in the eyewitnessed, bodily coming of the Word of life (1 John 1:1).

It gives tests of true faith: obedience, brotherly love, and confessing Christ in the flesh.
Its purpose: “that ye may know that ye have eternal life” (1 John 5:13).

corruption_summary: Perfectionism twists “born of God sinneth not” into sinlessness in this life, while cheap assurance claims to know God while walking in darkness; the liberal reduces “God is love” to sentiment severed from truth and holiness.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors mishandle First John's teaching on sin and assurance. Perfectionism seizes on “whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin” to claim a sinless state in this life, ignoring that the same epistle says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” John teaches that the believer does not practise sin as the settled course of his life, not that he is sinless. The opposite error is a cheap assurance that professes to know God while walking in darkness and hating the brethren; John denies it outright: “he that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now.”

The liberal corruption fastens on “God is love” and severs it from the truth and holiness that surround it, making love a sentiment that asks nothing of doctrine or obedience and affirms all things. But John defines the love of God as keeping His commandments, and grounds it in the propitiation of the cross—“herein is love… that he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” The dictionary holds First John whole: God is love and God is light; the believer may know he has eternal life; and that knowledge is confirmed, not contradicted, by obedience, brotherly love, and the confession that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh.

pos: noun phrase (the fall of the northern kingdom)
etymology: From Assyria, the empire that conquered the northern kingdom of Israel; the deportation of the ten tribes in 722 B.C. as judgment for their apostasy.
biblical_def: The Assyrian captivity was the conquest of the northern kingdom of Israel and the deportation of its people by the Assyrian empire in 722 B.C., a judgment of God upon the ten tribes for their long apostasy. In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria took Samaria and carried Israel away into Assyria, settling them in Halah, in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes. The inspired historian does not leave the cause in doubt: “For so it was, that the children of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God… and had feared other gods.” From the day Jeroboam set up the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, the northern kingdom never departed from that idolatry; king after king did evil, the people served Baal and the high places, and they rejected the warnings the LORD sent by all His servants the prophets. Therefore the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them out of His sight, until there was none left but the tribe of Judah only. The dictionary holds the Assyrian captivity as a sober witness to the certainty of divine judgment upon covenant unfaithfulness: God is longsuffering, sending prophet after prophet, but His patience has a term, and persistent idolatry brings at last the threatened curse. It marks the event against the sentimental denial that God judges nations and against the idle speculation about the “lost ten tribes,” which Scripture treats not as a mystery to be solved but as a people scattered in judgment. The captivity stands as a perpetual warning that the same God who blesses obedience visits the sins of a people who forsake Him.
webster_summary: The conquest of the northern kingdom of Israel and the deportation of the ten tribes by Assyria in 722 B.C. (2 Kings 17:6), the judgment of God for their persistent idolatry; a sober witness to the certainty of judgment on covenant unfaithfulness.

The king of Assyria took Samaria and carried Israel into Assyria (2 Kings 17:6).

The LORD removed Israel out of His sight; none was left but Judah (2 Kings 17:18).

Until the LORD removed Israel out of his sight, as he had said by all his servants the prophets. So was Israel carried away out of their own land to Assyria unto this day.

corruption_summary: Sentimentalism denies that God judges nations for sin, while idle speculation turns the deported tribes into a mystery of “lost ten tribes” foreign to the text's plain account of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of God's judgment upon covenant unfaithfulness. The sentimental theology of the age denies that God judges peoples and nations for their sin, preferring a deity who only blesses and never chastises. The inspired historian permits no such evasion: the LORD was very angry with Israel and removed them out of His sight, naming their idolatry as the cause. The Assyrian captivity stands as a sober and perpetual witness that divine patience, though long, has a term, and that persistent rebellion brings at last the threatened curse.

A second and idler corruption turns the deported tribes into the romantic mystery of the “lost ten tribes,” the seedbed of much speculation and not a little heresy (British-Israelism and the like). The dictionary declines the speculation. Scripture treats the scattered northern tribes not as a riddle to be solved by tracing them to distant nations, but as a people dispersed in judgment, a remnant of whom returned and mingled with Judah. The captivity's lesson is moral and theological, not genealogical: God judged His people for forsaking Him, and the same God still calls nations and churches to fear Him, lest the candlestick be removed.
roots_summary: From Assyria, the Mesopotamian empire of Nineveh; the “captivity” (Hebrew galah, to be carried into exile) of the northern ten tribes, distinct from the later Babylonian captivity of Judah.

Distinct from the Babylonian captivity of Judah a century and a half later.

He declined the speculation of the “lost ten tribes,” reading the text's plain account of judgment.
She heard in Samaria's fall a warning to every church that forsakes its first love.

etymology: A traditional name for the intertestamental period between the prophecy of Malachi and the coming of John the Baptist, when no canonical prophet spoke in Israel.
biblical_def: The four hundred silent years are the intertestamental period—roughly four centuries between the last canonical prophet, Malachi, and the appearance of John the Baptist—during which no inspired prophet spoke the word of the LORD in Israel. They are “silent” not because nothing happened (these were the eventful years of Persian, Greek, and Roman dominion, of the Maccabees, the rise of the synagogue, and the parties of Pharisees and Sadducees) but because the voice of canonical prophecy was stilled, as Amos had foretold a famine, not of bread, but of hearing the words of the LORD. Malachi himself had sealed the Old Testament with a promise that bridged the silence: “Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me”; and “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD.” When at last the silence broke, it broke with the cry of John the Baptist in the wilderness, the promised messenger preparing the way, and then with the Word made flesh. The dictionary holds the silent years as a witness to the providence of God ordering history toward the fulness of time: through them He prepared the world—the synagogue, the Greek tongue, the dispersion, the Roman roads—for the swift spread of the gospel. It marks the period against two errors: the elevation of the apocryphal and intertestamental writings of these years to the level of canonical Scripture, which the dictionary rejects as the Protestant canon does; and the despairing notion that God had abandoned His people, when in truth He was silently arranging the stage for the greatest act of redemptive history, the coming of His Son.
webster_summary: The intertestamental period of about four centuries between Malachi and John the Baptist, when no canonical prophet spoke (Amos 8:11); broken at last by the promised messenger (Malachi 3:1), the silence in which God prepared the world for the fulness of time.

“Silent” in that no canonical prophet spoke the word of the LORD (Amos 8:11).

corruption_summary: One error elevates the apocryphal writings of these years to canonical Scripture; the other reads the silence as God's abandonment, when in truth He was preparing the world for the fulness of time.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One live error concerns the canon. During the silent years arose the apocryphal and intertestamental writings—Maccabees, Tobit, Judith, Sirach, and the rest—which Rome received into its canon at Trent. The dictionary holds the Protestant canon: these books, however useful for history, are not inspired Scripture, and their very period is marked by the absence of the prophetic voice. The silence of those years is itself a witness that the Old Testament canon was closed with Malachi until the new prophetic dawn in John and in Christ.

The opposite error reads the silence as the abandonment of God, as though He had forgotten His people through four long centuries. The dictionary answers that the silence was not absence but preparation. Through those years the providence of God ordered the world for the gospel: the synagogue taught the Scriptures, the Greek tongue gave a common speech, the dispersion scattered worshippers of the true God among the nations, and Rome built the roads the apostles would walk. The silence ended exactly as Malachi promised, with the messenger preparing the way; and the four hundred years of waiting proved to be the ripening of the fulness of time for the coming of the Son.
roots_summary: From the “silence” of canonical prophecy between Malachi and John; the “intertestamental” period named for its place between the two Testaments.
roots_lines: “Silent”: no canonical prophet spoke the word of the LORD in these centuries.
“Intertestamental”: the period between the Old and New Testaments.
Amos' “famine… of hearing the words of the LORD” foretells the silence (Amos 8:11).
Malachi's promise of the messenger bridges the silence (Malachi 3:1).
Broken by John the Baptist, the promised forerunner.

pos: noun phrase (the timing of the crucifixion)
etymology: From “crucifixion” and “chronology” (Greek chronos, time); the sequence and timing of the events of Christ's death, as recorded in the Gospels.
biblical_def: The crucifixion chronology is the sequence and timing of the events of our Lord's death as recorded by the four evangelists—the hours of the day, the darkness, and the relation to the Passover. Mark marks the progress: it was the third hour when they crucified Him; at the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour; and at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” and gave up the ghost. John, who often reckons by a different scheme, notes that it was the preparation of the passover, about the sixth hour, when Pilate presented Him: “Behold your King!” The supernatural darkness from noon to three, the rending of the temple veil, and the death at the time of the evening sacrifice all belong to the solemn order of that day. The dictionary holds the crucifixion chronology as a matter of the Gospels' historical accuracy and harmony, and as a window into the meaning of the cross. The apparent differences between Mark's “third hour” and John's “sixth hour” are reasonably explained by differing reckonings of time (Jewish from sunrise, Roman or Johannine from midnight) or by the rounding of hours, and do not amount to contradiction; the faithful harmonist finds the accounts complementary, not opposed. The dictionary marks the chronology against the critical assumption that such differences prove the Gospels unreliable, and against the idle over-precision that builds doctrines on a disputed hour. What is sure and central is the substance: at the time of sacrifice, in supernatural darkness, the Lamb of God bore the wrath of God for His people and died, that the veil might be rent and the way into the holiest opened.
webster_summary: The sequence and timing of Christ's death in the Gospels—the third, sixth, and ninth hours, the darkness, the Passover (Mark 15:25-34; John 19:14); the apparent hour-differences harmonized by differing reckonings, against the claim that they prove the Gospels unreliable.
webster_full: CRUCIFIXION CHRONOLOGY, noun phrase. The sequence and timing of the events of Christ's death in the Gospels.
“It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 15:25).
Darkness covered the land from the sixth to the ninth hour (Mark 15:33).
At the ninth hour He cried, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34).
John notes the preparation of the passover, about the sixth hour (John 19:14).
scriptures: And it was the third hour, and they crucified him.
And when the sixth hour was come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.
And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
And it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your King!
corruption_summary: The critical school treats the apparent hour-differences as proof that the Gospels contradict and are unreliable, while an idle over-precision builds doctrines on a disputed hour.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the harmony and reliability of the Gospels. The critical school seizes on the apparent difference between Mark's “third hour” of the crucifixion and John's “sixth hour” at the judgment as proof that the evangelists contradict and that Scripture errs. The dictionary answers that the difference is reasonably resolved: the evangelists may reckon hours by differing conventions (the Jewish day from sunrise, the Johannine perhaps from midnight), and ancient reckoning rounded to the nearest third of the day. The accounts are complementary witnesses, not contradictions; the faithful reader harmonizes rather than impugns.

The opposite error is an idle over-precision that builds large conclusions on a disputed hour or insists on a rigid timetable the texts do not supply. The dictionary counsels sobriety here too: the Gospels were not written to satisfy the stopwatch but to bear true witness, and they agree in all that matters. What is sure and central is the substance of the day—the supernatural darkness from noon to three, the cry of dereliction, the death at the hour of the evening sacrifice, the rending of the veil. On these the four agree, and on these the dictionary rests: the Lamb of God died in darkness, bearing the wrath of God, and opened the way into the holiest.
roots_summary: From chronos (time) applied to the crucifixion; the Gospels mark the “hours” (Greek hora) of the day, reckoned by differing conventions.
roots_lines: Hora, Greek, “hour,” the divisions of the daylight reckoned in the Gospels.
The Jewish day was counted from sunrise; the “third hour” thus near nine in the morning.
John may reckon from midnight, placing the “sixth hour” near dawn.
The darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour (noon to three) was supernatural.
The death near the ninth hour coincided with the time of the evening sacrifice.
usage: The teacher harmonized Mark's and John's hours by differing conventions of reckoning time.

pos: noun phrase (the preaching of the church fathers)
etymology: From “patristic” (Latin pater, father) and “preaching”; the proclamation of the word by the fathers of the early church, of whom Chrysostom and Augustine are chief.
biblical_def: Patristic preaching is the proclamation of the word of God by the fathers of the early church, the homiletical heritage of the first centuries, of which the expository sermons of John Chrysostom and the discourses of Augustine of Hippo are the great examples. The fathers, for all their differences and errors, held to the apostolic charge: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.” They knew that it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe, and that faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God; how then should men believe in Him of whom they have not heard, and how hear without a preacher? Chrysostom, the “golden-mouthed,” preached consecutively through whole books of Scripture, expounding the text and applying it with searching power to the consciences of his hearers—a model of expository preaching the Reformers admired and revived. The dictionary commends what is commendable in patristic preaching: its high view of the word, its expository labour, its boldness against sin even in emperors, and its pastoral earnestness. Yet it does not receive the fathers uncritically. Their preaching carried, in places, the allegorical excess of Alexandria, the rising errors of sacramentalism and the cult of the saints, and a growing accommodation to imperial Christianity. The dictionary applies its standing rule: honour what is honourable—the fathers' reverence for Scripture and their gifts in proclaiming it—while naming as error what departed from the apostolic faith. The fathers were faithful witnesses, never authoritative; their preaching is to be weighed by the Scripture they served, and the Reformers' recovery of plain, expository, Christ-centred preaching stands in the best of their line.
webster_summary: The preaching of the early church fathers, chiefly Chrysostom and Augustine; commended for its high view of the word and expository labour, yet weighed by Scripture and not received uncritically where it carried allegory or rising error.
webster_full: PATRISTIC PREACHING, noun phrase. [Latin pater, father.] The proclamation of the word by the early church fathers.
Held to the apostolic charge: “Preach the word… with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2 Timothy 4:2).
Chrysostom, the “golden-mouthed,” preached expositionally through whole books.
Admired and revived by the Reformers as a model of expository preaching.
Honoured where faithful, yet weighed by Scripture where it carried allegory or error.
scriptures: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: Patristic preaching is corrupted by uncritical veneration that treats the fathers as authoritative, and by the wholesale dismissal that despises the early church's genuine homiletical heritage.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption is the uncritical veneration that elevates the fathers to a near-authoritative status, receiving their sermons and opinions as a second rule beside Scripture. The dictionary, holding sola Scriptura, denies this: the fathers, however gifted and earnest, were faithful witnesses, not infallible authorities, and their preaching is to be weighed by the word they served. Their genuine errors—the allegorical excess inherited from Alexandria, the rising sacramentalism, the cult of the saints, the accommodation to imperial power—are not to be swallowed for the sake of their antiquity. Antiquity is not authority.

The opposite corruption is the modern dismissal that despises the early church entirely, as though nothing of value lay between the apostles and the Reformation. This too the dictionary refuses. Chrysostom's patient exposition of whole books, the fathers' high reverence for Scripture, their boldness in reproving sin even in emperors, and their pastoral earnestness are a heritage the Reformers gladly owned and revived. The dictionary applies its rule for non-Reformed figures: honour what is honourable, name the error as error. Patristic preaching at its best—the word expounded, Christ proclaimed, the conscience addressed—stands in the same line as the plain, expository, Christ-centred preaching the Reformation recovered.
roots_summary: From the Latin pater (father), whence “patristic” and “patristics”; the “fathers” are the teachers of the early church whose preaching shaped its homiletical tradition.
roots_lines: Pater, Latin, father, the root of “patristic” and “patristics.”
Homilia, Greek, a discourse or sermon, whence “homily.”
Chrysostom, “golden-mouthed,” the chief patristic expository preacher.
Augustine of Hippo, whose sermons and treatises shaped Western preaching.
Weighed by the apostolic charge to “preach the word” (2 Timothy 4:2).
